Writing Assembly 1
There are times when you actually have to code asm in order to do something from a C/C++ file
Fairly common in firmware, OS, or driver programming. Because there are many aspects of hardware which can only be accessed with special instructions
If you were making a crypto library, you would want access to hardware cryptographic acceleration instructions
Or maybe you just want full control over the code being generated for optimization purposes
Writing Assembly 2
Being able to write assembly is a great way to simply experiment with instructions we have, and haven't covered in this class
Though getting the syntax right for the desired instructions/assemblers is often annoying
Inline Assembly
Inline assembly is a way to include assembly directly in-place in a C/C++ file
GCC supports inline assembly in GNU Assembler (gas) syntax
VisualStudio supports inline assembly for 32-bit binaries, but discontinued support for 64-bit
Standalone Assembly 1
Pure assembly can be written in a standalone file, assembled by an assembler into an object file, and then linked into the final binary with other compiled objects
This is the required path for raw x86-64 assembly in Visual Studio
Standalone Assembly 2
Different assemblers have their own syntax variants and helper mechanisms to make programming in assembly less painful for those who must
MASM (Microsoft Assembler) is what's used with Visual Studio
NASM (Netwide Assembler) is cross-platform
Raw Bytes
Most inline/standalone assembly-writing solutions also have support for emitting raw bytes, which the processor will interpret as instructions
This can be a good way to check your understanding of how you think the manual is specifying a particular assembly instruction is encoded, vs. what a disassembler ultimately says you encoded
This can also be used to work around not knowing the correct syntax for some instruction in some assembler
